newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Southern African trade bloc to raise productivity.
newsitem.headline: Southern African trade bloc to raise productivity.

text.p: European donor-country representatives said on Sunday they supported the drive by Southern African states to increase productivity in the region and to create a free trade area.

The 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) began meeting in the Namibian capital Windhoek on Monday for a 10-day annual conference, under the theme "Productivity", to consider ways of pooling resources to boost the region's economic growth.

"The choice of conference themes over the years has become more and more related to the real issues of the economy," Francisco da Camara, head of the Southern Africa division at the European Commission, told Reuters.
"SADC is changing its nature. It's not a coordinating conference any more. They're aiming at creating community, they're looking for economic integration."
The European Union also funds many projects that have a direct impact on integration.
"It is clear that the ultimate creation of an internal market can boost productivity levels enormously," Dutch Development Cooperation Minister Jan Pronk said in his statement on behalf of the EU.
SADC has given itself eight years to accomplish the creation of a free trade area expected to comprise 150 million people.

South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo, chairman of the SADC Council of Ministers, said outstanding progress had been made in the process towards regional integration through the signing of several protocols.
"The trade protocol in particular will be the main engine that drives economic integration in Southern Africa," he said.
But ratification of the protocol, which aims at a phased reduction of tariffs, is slow and the Council of Ministers urged member states this week to speed up the process.

"Some countries are awaiting the conclusion of technical work on the redcution of tariffs and feel that one has to conclude those negotiations before they can ratify the trade protocol," SADC executive secretary Kaire Mbuende said.

But Pronk warned: "If you create an internal market in a region marked by great differences between the various countries, there is an increased risk of a widening trade gap to the benefit of the economically more powerful member states."

The trade imbalances within SADC are already huge. And since the region's strongest economic power, South Africa, has taken over the SADC chairmanship for the next three years, it will have to balance its own trading interest with the interests of the region as a whole.
SADC comprises Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi, South Africa and Botswana.
